title: The Lioness and the Vixen
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Lioness and a Vixen were talking together about their young, as mothers will, and saying how healthy and well-grown they were, and what beautiful coats they had, and how they were the image of their parents. "My litter of cubs is a joy to see," said the Fox; and then she added, rather maliciously, "But I notice you never have more than one." "No," said the Lioness grimly, "but that one's a lion." Quality, not quantity.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who are the two animals talking together?
options: A Tigress and a Wolf
A Lioness and a Bear
A Lioness and a Vixen
A Vixen and a Panther

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the two mothers say about their young?
options: That they were sickly and small
That they looked nothing like their parents
That they refused to eat
That they were healthy, well-grown, and the image of their parents

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fox say about her litter of cubs?
options: That it is too large to manage
That it is a joy to see
That it is smaller than the Lioness's
That it looks weak

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fox point out about the Lioness, rather maliciously?
options: That she never has more than one cub
That her cub is smaller than a fox cub
That she has no cubs at all
That her cub has an ugly coat

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "litter" mean in "my litter of cubs"?
options: Rubbish left on the ground
A type of stretcher
A group of animal young born at one time
A nesting material

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "maliciously" mean in "she added, rather maliciously"?
options: Cheerfully
Quietly
Honestly
With an intent to hurt or provoke

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Lioness's reply, "but that one's a lion," work as an effective comeback?
options: It proves the Lioness has more cubs than the Fox
It suggests that one exceptional offspring outweighs having many ordinary ones
It shows the Lioness cannot count her own cubs
It admits that the Fox's cubs are superior

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, as its closing line makes explicit?
options: Quality, not quantity, is what truly counts
Quantity always matters more than quality
Foxes are wiser than lions
Mothers should never compare their children

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does it say the two mothers do "as mothers will"?
options: Argue over territory
Compare their young
Hunt together
Groom each other's fur

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does it say about the coats of their young?
options: Ragged
Colorless
Unusually short
Beautiful

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does it describe the way the Lioness responds to the Fox's remark?
options: Cheerfully
Nervously
Grimly
Apologetically

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "grimly" mean in "said the Lioness grimly"?
options: In a stern or humorless manner
In a joyful tone
In a confused way
In a whisper

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Lioness's grim tone suggest about how she takes the Fox's jab?
options: She finds it amusing and laughs along
She is too distracted to respond properly
She agrees completely with the Fox
She takes it seriously enough to give a pointed, serious reply

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Lioness and a Fox argue over whose cubs have prettier coats
A Fox mocks a Lioness for having only one cub, but the Lioness replies that her one cub is a lion, making the point that quality outweighs quantity
A Fox and a Lioness raise their cubs together
A Lioness admits the Fox's cubs are better than her own
